---
title: "CPI Components"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(fbi)
library(psych)
library(kableExtra)
```

FRED-MD (McCracken and Ng) publishes three Consumer Price Index subcomponents:

- `CPIAPPSL`: Apparel
- `CPITRNSL`: Transportation
- `CPIMEDSL`: Medical Care

Each component has its own price driver: apparel tracks import costs and retail markdowns, transportation follows energy prices, medical care follows insurance and health policy. No mechanism links them month to month. But all three are nominal price indices, so all three trend upward for the same reason: aggregate inflation. That shared trend is the confound ECE strips out — the same role physically unrelated genomic probes play in `copy-number-variation.qmd`, sharing an instrument-calibration drift instead of an inflation drift. We test the joint null: the 3x3 correlation matrix is diagonal.

```{R cpi-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

fred_data <- fredmd(
  "../data/real-data/FRED-2026-05.csv",
  date_start = NULL, date_end = NULL, transform = FALSE
) |> as_tibble()

X_data <- fred_data |>
  select(date, CPIAPPSL, CPITRNSL, CPIMEDSL) |>
  drop_na() |>
  rename(
    `Apparel`        = CPIAPPSL,
    `Transportation` = CPITRNSL,
    `Medical Care`   = CPIMEDSL
  )

X_mat   <- as.matrix(X_data[, -1])
X_seg   <- segment_mean(X_mat, penalty = "BIC")
X_resid <- X_mat - X_seg
```

## Diagnostics

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R cpi-plot-raw}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-cpi-components
#| fig-cap: "CPI subcomponents, monthly levels, 1959-2026. Thick lines show the segmented mean."
#| fig-height: 7

X <- bind_cols(
  date = X_data$date, X_data[, -1],
  as.data.frame(X_seg) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment"))
)

X |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type     = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
    category = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = category, group = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.4, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "CPI Subcomponents", x = NULL, y = "Index level", color = "Category",
    caption = "Source: FRED-MD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

All three climb for six decades. Transportation is the most volatile, driven by energy shocks in 2008 and 2021-2022. Medical Care is the smoothest, climbing almost without pause.

## Trend

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Naive

Same 3x3 layout as the Mean-Shift-Invariant tab: the diagonal holds each series' rolling-mean-removed variance, the upper triangle holds the naive pairwise covariance term, the lower triangle is blank.

```{R cpi-trend-naive}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

R <- apply(X_mat, 2, function(col) col - rolling_mean(col, window))
idx_p <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

naive_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_p)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_p[1, k]
  j <- idx_p[2, k]
  s <- R[, i] * R[, j]
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
naive_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- R[, i] * R[, i]
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
naive_terms_dat <- bind_rows(naive_cov_dat, naive_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(naive_terms_dat, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "naive term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Mean-Shift-Invariant

`plot_ece_terms()` builds on `lag_term()`, which compares each point against its two predecessors through a circular shift (`rotate()`). A series that trends for 60+ years without cycling back pays for that shift at the boundary: the last couple of points wrap around and land against the 1959 starting level, producing a spike that swamps the rest of the y-axis. The layout below follows the same row/column convention as the Correlation tables: the diagonal holds each series' own variance term (`lag_term(X[,i], X[,i])`), the upper triangle holds the pairwise covariance term, and the lower triangle stays blank — redundant with the upper triangle.

```{R cpi-trend-ece-data}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

ece_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
ece_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
ece_terms_dat <- bind_rows(ece_cov_dat, ece_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn))
```

```{R cpi-trend-ece}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_trend <- ece_terms_dat |>
  filter(t > 2, t < n - 1) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_trend, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "ECE term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The large excursion around 2021 in all three panels is the COVID-era inflation shock, not an artifact. The boundary artifact is a separate problem: fewer points, larger magnitude, and still excluded from the plot above — excluded from the display only, since every `ece.test()` p-value elsewhere in this chapter runs on the full, untrimmed series. The histogram below restores those boundary points, showing the full term distribution on the same 3x3 layout (diagonal = variance term, upper triangle = covariance term), so the impact is visible directly rather than trimmed away.

```{R cpi-trend-hist}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_summary <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw), .groups = "drop")

ece_terms_trimmed <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  filter(raw > quantile(raw, 0.005), raw < quantile(raw, 0.995)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_trimmed, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = mean), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = median), color = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "ECE term value (middle 99%)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Almost every observation sits in a single bar near zero. The x-axis stretches to several hundred just to fit one or two boundary points per panel — the same points `bs_multiplier_test` and `bs_parametric_test` build their statistics from internally, since both call `ece_terms(X)` on this exact, untrimmed data. The mean (dashed red) and median (dashed orange) both sit near zero in every panel: the boundary points barely move the center of the distribution. They do move `sum(s_t^2)`, though, the quantity the bootstrap null variance is built from — a handful of points out of 807 is enough to shift that by an order of magnitude.

### Mean-Shift-Invariant (Segment)

Same terms as the Mean-Shift-Invariant tab (`lag_term()`, same 3x3 layout), computed on `X_resid` (the `segment_mean()` residuals) instead of the raw levels. This is the diagnostic behind the Segment-ECE row in the Results table below. With the trend already removed, `lag_term()` no longer sees a 60-year monotonic climb, so the `rotate()` boundary wraparound never produces the spike seen in the raw-level tab. The remaining large excursions — Transportation near t=600 and t=750, Medical Care near t=800 — line up with the 2008 and 2021-2022 energy and inflation shocks, not an artifact.

```{R cpi-trend-segment-ece}
#| echo: false

window <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat) / 5))
cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)

seg_ece_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
seg_ece_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
seg_ece_terms_dat <- bind_rows(seg_ece_cov_dat, seg_ece_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), global = mean(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(seg_ece_terms_dat, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = global), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "time", y = "Segment-ECE term (covariance / variance scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::

## Kappa

The default pairwise z-test (`ece.test(..., type = "z.test")`) uses `kappa = "gaussian"`: a delta-method standard error that assumes the fourth-moment terms take their Gaussian values (`k40 = k04 = 3`, `k22 = 1 + 2ρ²`, `k31 = k13 = 3ρ`), with the correlation `ρ` plugged in at its estimated value. We check that assumption directly, estimating these terms from the segmented residuals (`ece.kappa(..., method = "mom")`):

```{R cpi-kappa-check}
#| echo: false

cn  <- colnames(X_mat)
idx <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

kappa_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(
    Pair = paste(cn[i], "/", cn[j]),
    k40  = round(kap$k40, 2),
    k31  = round(kap$k31, 2),
    k22  = round(kap$k22, 2),
    k13  = round(kap$k13, 2),
    k04  = round(kap$k04, 2)
  )
})

kable(kappa_tbl, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Under a Gaussian sampling check (iid `rnorm`, same n=807, 50 replicates), these estimators center near the Gaussian reference values with modest spread (`k40`, `k04`: mean 3.0, sd ~0.4; `k22`: mean 1.0, sd ~0.16). The estimates above sit far outside that range. For the two pairs involving `Apparel` and `Transportation`, `k40`/`k04` reach 15-20 against a reference of 3, and `k22` reaches 4.05 against a reference near 1. `Medical Care`'s own marginal term (`k04` in the last two rows) stays closer to Gaussian, at 1.78. The `kappa = "gaussian"` z-test understates the true standard error for these pairs — its p-values run lower than the bootstrap methods (`bs.multiplier`, `bs.parametric`) agree with.

**Fix: test under the null instead of estimating all five kappas.** `ece.cor.se()` forces `ρ = 0` when `rho = 0` is passed. Every kappa term with a nonzero coefficient in the SE formula — `k40`, `k04`, `k31`, `k13` — carries a factor of `ρ` or `ρ²`, so at `ρ = 0` they all drop out algebraically. Only `k22` remains, and under true independence it collapses to exactly 1 for any marginal distribution, not just Gaussian. This is standard practice: a test of H0: ρ=0 should use the standard error *at* ρ=0, not one built from the plug-in estimate of ρ.

The Results section below uses this null-restricted z-test — `kappa = ece.kappa(X, rho = 0, method = "mom")`, `rho = 0` — instead of the full Gaussian one, so it only has to estimate `k22` rather than assume all five kappas take their Gaussian values. Every pairwise p-value moves toward the bootstrap methods' answer, though not all the way there. `Apparel`'s residual autocorrelation (lag-1 ACF of 0.44) is a second factor no z-test variant addresses, since `ece.cor.se()` carries no lag terms at all. All three tests here — z-test, `bs.multiplier`, `bs.parametric` — assume the underlying series is independent over time. The bootstrap tests' lag-1/lag-2 correction is calibrated to the dependence `lag_term()`'s own construction mechanically induces, not to arbitrary leftover autocorrelation in the data.

## Omega

This chapter residualizes the trend throughout with `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")`, for Segment-ECE and the residualized joint tests in Results. It's one reasonable change-point fit, not a known-true segmentation. We check how well it describes the actual mean-shift structure using ECE itself. `ece.complexity()` estimates $\omega$ — the mean-heterogeneity parameter from `omega-estimation.qmd` — directly from the raw data via lagged differences, with no change-point model at all. If the segmentation fits well, the same $\omega$ quantity computed from the fitted segmented mean (`lag_diff(X_seg[,i], X_seg[,j]) / n`, the same construction `omega-estimation.qmd` uses for the true mean process) should closely match ECE's own estimate.

```{R cpi-omega-check}
#| echo: false

n <- nrow(X_mat)
cn <- colnames(X_mat)

ece_omega <- ece.complexity(X_mat) |> round(1)
rownames(ece_omega) <- colnames(ece_omega) <- cn

seg_omega <- matrix(0, ncol(X_mat), ncol(X_mat), dimnames = list(cn, cn))
for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
    seg_omega[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_seg[, i], X_seg[, j], k = 1) / n
  }
}
seg_omega <- round(seg_omega, 1)
```

```{R cpi-omega-check-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_omega, caption = "ECE (raw data, no segmentation)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega, caption = "Segmentation-implied")
```

The two agree to within 0.1-2.2% on every entry — independent corroboration of the segmentation choice. `ece.complexity()` requires no change-point model at all, built the same way as the correlation and variance terms throughout this chapter, yet it recovers essentially the same mean-heterogeneity structure as the explicit `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` fit. That doesn't make the BIC segmentation the "right" one in any absolute sense. It does mean two independent descriptions of this data's mean-shift structure — ECE's differencing-based estimator and an explicit change-point model — aren't in tension.

:::

## Results

We start with pairwise comparisons: ECE and Segment-ECE — ECE applied to the raw levels and to the `segment_mean()` residuals — alongside naive and residual Pearson correlation, the same two versions of the data run through Pearson.

```{R cpi-pairwise-cor}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

ece_cor               <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor)     <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)
seg_ece_cor           <- ece.cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
rownames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

resid_cor   <- cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

# Null-restricted z-test (rho = 0): avoids assuming Gaussian k40/k04/k31/k13,
# which the Kappa diagnostic tab shows are badly misspecified for this data.
ece_pval_null <- function(X) {
  p <- ncol(X)
  pval_mat <- matrix(NA, p, p)
  colnames(pval_mat) <- rownames(pval_mat) <- colnames(X)
  for (i in 1:(p - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):p) {
      pair <- cbind(X[, i], X[, j])
      pval <- ece.test(pair, type = "z.test", kappa = ece.kappa(pair, rho = 0, method = "mom"), rho = 0)$p.value
      pval_mat[i, j] <- pval
      pval_mat[j, i] <- pval
    }
  }
  diag(pval_mat) <- 0
  pval_mat
}

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval_null(X_mat) |> round(3)
seg_ece_pmat <- ece_pval_null(X_resid) |> round(3)
resid_pmat   <- cor_pval(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)

# Bold any off-diagonal cell whose corresponding p-value is < 0.05.
bold_sig <- function(display_mat, pval_mat) {
  m   <- nrow(display_mat)
  out <- matrix("", m, m, dimnames = dimnames(display_mat))
  for (i in seq_len(m)) {
    for (j in seq_len(m)) {
      sig <- i != j && !is.na(pval_mat[i, j]) && pval_mat[i, j] < 0.05
      out[i, j] <- kableExtra::cell_spec(sprintf("%.3f", display_mat[i, j]), "html", bold = sig)
    }
  }
  out
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Correlation

```{R cpi-pairwise-cor-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_cor, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_cor, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_cor, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_cor, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

Bold marks pairs significant at p < 0.05: correlation cells bold when the matching p-value clears it, p-value cells bold when they clear it themselves.

## P-Values

```{R cpi-pairwise-pval-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_pmat, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_pmat, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_pmat, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_pmat, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

:::

Naive Pearson correlation on the raw levels runs 0.77-0.98 across all three pairs (p < 0.001 for every pair). Residualizing against the segmented mean collapses that almost entirely, to 0.04-0.07, with p-values of 0.05-0.26. The pairwise ECE correlation on the raw levels is `NaN` for every pair: `ece.cov()`'s diagonal entries come out negative on these smooth, slow-moving levels, leaving `cov2cor()` no valid variance to divide by. This is the same boundary artifact from the Trend diagnostic above (`rotate()`'s circular wraparound), now showing up directly in the pairwise estimator rather than just the histogram.

Applying ECE to the segmented residuals instead (Segment-ECE) sidesteps that problem: 0.13-0.22, closer to naive Pearson than to residual Pearson. These p-values use the null-restricted z-test (see the Kappa tab in Diagnostics) rather than the full Gaussian one. Under it, Apparel/Transportation still rejects independence (p = 0.032); Apparel/Medical Care (p = 0.089) and Transportation/Medical Care (p = 0.091) no longer do. Both were flagged as significant under the full Gaussian z-test (p = 0.047, 0.073), and both drop out once the Gaussian kappa assumption is relaxed. We still lack a usable pairwise ECE correlation on the raw levels for this dataset — the joint diagonal tests below don't share that instability, and are the reliable read.

The Omega tab in Diagnostics checks whether the `segment_mean()` fit used throughout this chapter — for Segment-ECE and the residualized joint tests below — is corroborated by ECE's own segmentation-free estimator. It is.

We run all four tests on the raw levels, then again on `X_resid` — the same segmented residuals used for Segment-ECE above — as a check.

```{R cpi-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat), nrow(X_mat))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid), nrow(X_resid))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{R cpi-diagonal-tests-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(results,     caption = "Raw Levels")
knitr::kable(results_seg, caption = "Segmented Residuals")
```

On the raw levels (left), the Bartlett test and the naive parametric bootstrap — neither accounts for the mean shift — reject the diagonal null outright. The bootstrap multiplier and the mean-shift-aware parametric bootstrap both fail to reject: p = 0.18 and p = 0.41. These raw-level tests carry the `rotate()` boundary artifact from the Trend diagnostic: the last point or two get compared against the 1959 starting level, producing term values in the hundreds against a typical magnitude near zero. This already made the pairwise ECE correlation `NaN`. It also makes `bs.multiplier` mildly trim-sensitive here — p ranges 0.06-0.20 across boundary trims of 0-10 rows, "fail to reject" throughout but not a fixed number.

On the segmented residuals (right), all four tests fail to reject: 0.34, 0.17, 0.35, 0.09. This confirms rather than adds a finding. `bs.multiplier` and `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` are mean-shift-robust by construction — they cancel trend internally via lagged differences, and already reached "fail to reject" on the raw levels with no pre-processing. Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap have no such mechanism. Fed the raw levels, they mistake the shared trend for correlation and reject outright. Once we remove the trend for them by hand, subtracting a `segment_mean()` fit, they agree with the other two.

That fit is not an oracle. It's one reasonable change-point model (BIC-penalized), not a known-true segmentation, so this isn't "the right answer confirmed by ground truth." What it shows is narrower: the raw-level rejections from Bartlett and the naive bootstrap were an artifact of the shared trend, since removing that trend by an entirely different route — explicit segmentation instead of ECE's internal differencing — makes the rejection go away. The headline result stays the raw-level table, where `bs.multiplier` and `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` reach "no correlation" directly, with no change-point model required. The residualized table is the check confirming that answer wasn't a fluke.

## Downsampling

At monthly resolution, Apparel's residual lag-1 ACF is 0.44 — high enough to check whether coarser sampling helps, and whether the diagonal-test conclusions hold up if it does. We compare monthly against striding every 2nd month (bi-monthly, n=404) and every 3rd month (quarterly, n=269), using the same `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` residualization at each resolution.

```{R cpi-downsample}
#| echo: false

X_bimonthly <- X_mat[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 2), ]
X_quarterly <- X_mat[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 3), ]
dates_bi    <- X_data$date[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 2)]
dates_q     <- X_data$date[seq(1, nrow(X_mat), by = 3)]

X_bimonthly_seg   <- segment_mean(X_bimonthly, penalty = "BIC")
X_quarterly_seg   <- segment_mean(X_quarterly, penalty = "BIC")
X_bimonthly_resid <- X_bimonthly - X_bimonthly_seg
X_quarterly_resid <- X_quarterly - X_quarterly_seg

acf1 <- function(X) {
  X_resid <- X - segment_mean(X, penalty = "BIC")
  round(apply(X_resid, 2, function(v) acf(v, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]), 2)
}

downsample_row <- function(X, label) {
  a <- acf1(X)
  set.seed(123)
  data.frame(
    Resolution = label, n = nrow(X),
    `ACF (Apparel/Transportation/Medical)` = paste(a, collapse = " / "),
    `Bootstrap Multiplier` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    `Parametric Bootstrap` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    `Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)` = round(ece.test(X, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    `Bartlett Test` = signif(cortest.bartlett(cor(X), nrow(X))$p.value, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

downsample_results <- bind_rows(
  downsample_row(X_mat, "Monthly"),
  downsample_row(X_bimonthly, "Bi-monthly"),
  downsample_row(X_quarterly, "Quarterly")
)

kable(downsample_results, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Coarser sampling brings Apparel's ACF down (0.44 to 0.29 to 0.14), but it doesn't move monotonically toward zero for the other two: Transportation runs -0.09 to -0.26 to -0.33, Medical Care runs 0.00 to -0.38 to -0.64. Downsampling trades a moderate positive autocorrelation for a larger negative one.

```{R cpi-downsample-helpers}
plot_downsample_raw <- function(X, X_seg, dates, title) {

  X_df |>

plot_downsample_resid <- function(X_resid, dates, title) {

}

acf_naive_plot <- function(X_resid) {
  par(mfrow = c(ncol(X_resid), 1), mar = c(0, 3, 0, 1), oma = c(4, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))

  }
  axis(1)

}
```

More importantly, the two mean-shift-aware tests stop agreeing once we downsample. `Parametric Bootstrap` (`lag1.diag.psd`) fails to reject at every resolution — 0.41, 0.39, 0.48 — stable regardless of n or stride. `Bootstrap Multiplier` fails to reject at monthly resolution (p = 0.18), but rejects at both bi-monthly and quarterly, at p-values from 1e-3 to 1e-17 depending on the bootstrap seed. Both of those count as "reject" at any conventional level; the seed-to-seed spread isn't the interesting part. What matters is that the rejection appears exactly when we downsample and is absent at monthly resolution, while `lag1.diag.psd`'s answer doesn't move.

We haven't identified why `bs.multiplier` behaves this way under downsampling. It could be an artifact of how it re-splits a shorter series internally, a real sensitivity to something downsampling changes beyond the ACF (fixing the ACF didn't fix it), or something else. We report it rather than pick a resolution that hides it.

---

Where this leaves us: apparel, transportation, and medical care prices have no known mechanism linking their month-to-month movements. At monthly resolution, every mean-shift-aware test agrees. Both the bootstrap multiplier and the mean-shift-aware parametric bootstrap fail to reject the diagonal null, while Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap reject confidently — at essentially the same significance level as the two mean-shift-related sector correlations in `labor-productivity.qmd` that *are* real. That's the headline result: naive Pearson and Bartlett can't tell a shared secular trend from real contemporaneous correlation, and here domain knowledge tells us which one this is.

The downsampling check complicates this picture rather than confirming it: the parametric bootstrap's conclusion holds up across resolution, the bootstrap multiplier's does not, and we don't yet know why. Take the monthly result as this chapter's primary finding, and the resolution-dependence of `bs.multiplier` as an open question about the method, not about this dataset.

## Log-Transformed

Everything above runs on raw index levels — the same approach `pce-components.qmd` tries first and abandons, because dollar levels over-segment and break `ece.cor()` outright (see that chapter's "Raw Levels: An Initial Attempt"). CPI's raw-level analysis doesn't hit that failure mode: `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` finds a handful of genuine trend breaks rather than fitting local noise, and the pairwise/joint results above are usable. Still, log-differencing is standard economic convention — growth *rates*, not index levels, are the meaningful unit for prices — and it's the transformation used throughout `pce-components.qmd`. This section repeats the diagnostics and Results tables on log-differenced CPI data, to see whether the transformation changes either the diagnostics or the conclusions. On this transformed scale, `penalty = "BIC"` finds no change points at all — too conservative for growth-rate-sized shifts — and a single blanket `penalty = "AIC"` would still just be a guess at the right sensitivity. Instead, segmentation below picks a separate `pen.value` for each series, chosen so that series' segmentation-implied $\omega$ (the diagonal Omega-tab quantity, `lag_diff(seg, seg, k = 1) / n`) matches ECE's own segmentation-free estimate, `ece.complexity(x, x)`, as closely as possible — grid-searched over `10^seq(-8, 0, length.out = 100)`. Because `ece.complexity(x, x)` depends only on series `x` itself, this search is independent across the three series: each gets its own `pen.value`, chosen without reference to the other two.

```{R cpi-log-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

X_data_log <- fred_data |>
  select(date, CPIAPPSL, CPITRNSL, CPIMEDSL) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Apparel        = c(NA, diff(log(CPIAPPSL))),
    Transportation = c(NA, diff(log(CPITRNSL))),
    `Medical Care` = c(NA, diff(log(CPIMEDSL)))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Apparel)) |>
  select(date, Apparel, Transportation, `Medical Care`)

X_mat_log <- as.matrix(X_data_log[, -1])

# Per-series penalty search: choose pen.value so the segmentation-implied
# omega (diagonal, variance scale) matches ECE's own segmentation-free
# estimate as closely as possible. ece.complexity(x, x) depends only on
# column x, so each series is optimized independently of the other two.
pen_grid_log <- 10^seq(-8, 0, length.out = 100)

omega_match_penalty <- function(x, grid) {
  target <- ece.complexity(x, x)
  errs <- sapply(grid, function(pv) {
    seg       <- segment_mean_vec(x, penalty = "Manual", pen.value = pv)
    seg_omega <- lag_diff(seg, seg, k = 1) / length(x)
    abs(seg_omega - target) / abs(target)
  })
  grid[which.min(errs)]
}

pen_log <- apply(X_mat_log, 2, omega_match_penalty, grid = pen_grid_log)

X_seg_log <- sapply(colnames(X_mat_log), function(cn) {
  segment_mean_vec(X_mat_log[, cn], penalty = "Manual", pen.value = pen_log[cn])
})
colnames(X_seg_log) <- colnames(X_mat_log)
X_resid_log <- X_mat_log - X_seg_log
```

```{R cpi-log-penalty-table}
#| echo: false

n_segs_log <- apply(X_seg_log, 2, function(c) length(unique(c)))

penalty_tbl_log <- tibble(
  Series      = colnames(X_mat_log),
  `pen.value` = signif(pen_log, 3),
  Segments    = n_segs_log
)

kable(penalty_tbl_log, align = c("l", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

`r nrow(X_data_log)` monthly log growth-rate observations (one fewer than the raw-level series, lost to differencing).

```{R cpi-log-trend-ece-data}
#| echo: false

window_log <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat_log) / 5))
cn_log      <- colnames(X_mat_log)
idx_log     <- combn(ncol(X_mat_log), 2)
n_log       <- nrow(X_mat_log)

ece_cov_log <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_log)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_log[1, k]
  j <- idx_log[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat_log[, i], X_mat_log[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n_log), row = cn_log[i], col = cn_log[j], raw = s)
})
ece_var_log <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat_log)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_mat_log[, i], X_mat_log[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n_log), row = cn_log[i], col = cn_log[i], raw = s)
})
ece_terms_log <- bind_rows(ece_cov_log, ece_var_log) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn_log), col = factor(col, levels = cn_log)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window_log), mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ece_terms_log_labels <- ece_terms_log |> distinct(row, col, mean, median)
```

```{R cpi-log-trend-ece}
#| echo: false

ggplot(ece_terms_log, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = median), linetype = "dashed", color = "darkorange") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "time", y = "ECE term (covariance / variance scale)",
    subtitle = sprintf("gray = raw term, blue = %d-window mean, red = mean, orange = median", window_log)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Unlike the raw-level Trend tab above, there's no 60-year monotonic climb for `rotate()`'s circular boundary wraparound to catch — mean and median track each other closely in every panel, with no single point dominating the way the raw-level boundary artifact did.

```{R cpi-log-kappa-check}
cn_log_k  <- colnames(X_mat_log)

kappa_tbl_log <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_log_k)), function(k) {

  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid_log[, i], X_resid_log[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(

})

  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Compare against the raw-level Kappa table above. As on the raw levels, we use the null-restricted z-test (`rho = 0`) for the Results tables below, rather than assume these Gaussian reference values hold.

## Omega

```{R cpi-log-omega-check}
#| echo: false

n_log_o  <- nrow(X_mat_log)
cn_log_o <- colnames(X_mat_log)

ece_omega_log <- ece.complexity(X_mat_log) |> round(6)
rownames(ece_omega_log) <- colnames(ece_omega_log) <- cn_log_o

seg_omega_log <- matrix(0, ncol(X_mat_log), ncol(X_mat_log), dimnames = list(cn_log_o, cn_log_o))
for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_log))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_log))) {
    seg_omega_log[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_seg_log[, i], X_seg_log[, j], k = 1) / n_log_o
  }
}
seg_omega_log <- round(seg_omega_log, 6)
```

```{R cpi-log-omega-check-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_omega_log, caption = "ECE (log growth, no segmentation)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega_log, caption = "Segmentation-implied (log growth)")
```

Unlike the raw-level Omega check above, close agreement on the diagonal here isn't independent corroboration — the diagonal is exactly what the per-series `pen.value` search targeted, so `seg_omega_log`'s diagonal is expected to sit close to `ece_omega_log`'s by construction. The honest check is the off-diagonal (covariance-scale) entries: the search never had visibility into any pairwise term, only each series' own variance-scale $\omega$, so agreement there — or lack of it — is a genuine, uncontrived signal about whether a segmentation chosen purely from single-series information also happens to describe the joint mean-shift structure. Both estimates also run several orders of magnitude smaller than the raw-level Omega check above (that comparison was on the order of 1-100; this one is on the order of 1e-4 to 1e-6) — expected, since differencing removes the six-decade compounding trend that dominated the raw-level $\omega$.

```{R cpi-log-pairwise-cor-output}
knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_cor_log, ece_pmat_log),         caption = "ECE Correlation (Log Growth)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_cor_log, seg_ece_pmat_log), caption = "Segment-ECE Correlation (Log Growth)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_cor_log, pearson_pmat_log), caption = "Naive Pearson Correlation (Log Growth)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_cor_log, resid_pmat_log),     caption = "Residual Pearson Correlation (Log Growth)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

Bold marks pairs significant at p < 0.05, using the same null-restricted z-test (`ece_pval_null()`) as the raw-level Results section above.

```{R cpi-log-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results_log <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat_log, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_log, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_log, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat_log), nrow(X_mat_log))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg_log <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid_log, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_log, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_log, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid_log), nrow(X_resid_log))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{R cpi-log-diagonal-tests-output}
knitr::kable(results_log,     caption = "Log Growth, Raw")
knitr::kable(results_seg_log, caption = "Log Growth, Segmented Residuals")
```

---

Where this leaves the comparison: the raw-level analysis above needed `segment_mean()` residualization as a check precisely because the shared inflation trend is large enough to make Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap reject on the untransformed levels, and to make pairwise ECE correlation come out `NaN` from the `rotate()` boundary artifact. Log-differencing removes that trend before any test runs, the same fix `pce-components.qmd` reaches for on raw dollar levels. If the conclusions above and here agree, that's independent confirmation the raw-level headline result isn't an artifact of how ECE handles a strong shared trend; if they diverge, the divergence is itself informative about which transformation the joint-diagonal test is more sensitive to for this dataset.
